entry: American professional boxer and activist, widely known as "the Greatest." Born Cassius Clay in [[Louisville, Kentucky]], he won the world heavyweight title in 1964 by defeating Sonny Liston and then changed his name to Muhammad Ali. He had joined the [[Nation of Islam]] in the early 1960s and in the mid-1970s became a [[Sunni Islam|Sunni Muslim]]. In 1967 he refused induction into the military, citing religious beliefs and opposition to the [[Vietnam War]]. He was convicted of draft evasion and stripped of his boxing titles, but the Supreme Court overturned the conviction in 1971. He regained the title in 1974 by defeating [[George Foreman]] in the Rumble in the Jungle. Known for rhymed trash talk and an unorthodox style, he is identified as a pioneer of [[Hip-hop]]. He retired in 1981, and in 1984 he disclosed a diagnosis of Parkinson's syndrome.

[[Barrister]], statesman and founder of [[Pakistan]]. Born in Karachi and trained at Lincoln's Inn in London, he initially advocated Hindu–Muslim unity in the [[Indian National Congress]] and helped shape the 1916 Lucknow Pact. He resigned from the Congress in 1920 over its adoption of satyagraha, which he regarded as political anarchy. As leader of the All-India Muslim League from 1913, he argued that Muslims needed protection in a Hindu-dominated state, and in 1940 the League passed the Lahore Resolution. When the [[Partition of India]] created Pakistan on August 14, 1947, Jinnah became its first governor-general and personally supervised refugee camps for Muslim migrants. He died a year later. He is revered in Pakistan as the Quaid-e-Azam ("Great Leader") and Baba-e-Qaum ("Father of the Nation").

[[Ottoman Empire|Ottoman]] viceroy of Albanian origin and de facto ruler of Egypt from 1805 to 1848, widely considered the founder of modern Egypt. Born in a village in Albania, he served in an Albanian force sent to recover Egypt from the French after the withdrawal of [[Napoleon]]. Named wali (governor) of Egypt in 1805, he tried to modernize the military, economy and culture, and he purged the [[Mamluk|Mamluks]] to consolidate his rule. By 1840 his control extended over [[Sudan]], the Hejaz, the [[Levant]], Cyprus, Crete and parts of Greece. In 1831 he captured [[Syria]] and threatened [[Constantinople]] before European powers forced him to retreat. A brokered peace in 1842 granted him and his descendants hereditary rule over Egypt and Sudan. The dynasty ruled until the 1952 revolution, when King Farouk was overthrown by a movement led by Mohamed Naguib and [[Gamal Abdel Nasser]].

Islamic philosopher and poet, regarded as one of the most influential [[Urdu]] poets of the 20th century. Born in Sialkot, [[Punjab]], he studied at Government College in [[Lahore]] before going to England, where he earned a second BA at Trinity College, Cambridge, and qualified as a [[Barrister|barrister]]. He took a PhD in philosophy at Munich in 1908 with a thesis on metaphysics in Persia. His poems include *Asrar-e-Khudi* and *Bang-e-Dara*, and his [[Persian language|Persian]] works won him recognition in Iran. In 1930 his Allahabad Address, delivered at the League's annual assembly, outlined a political framework for the Muslim-majority regions of northwestern India, supporting the two-nation theory. He is honored in [[Pakistan]] as the national poet, and his birthday is a public holiday there.

Persian Tajik Muslim scholar and one of the foremost authorities on [[Hadith|hadith]], regarded as the most important hadith scholar in the history of [[Sunni Islam]]. Born in Bukhara, in present-day [[Uzbekistan]], he began studying hadith at age 10 and traveled widely through the [[Abbasid Caliphate]] in search of traditions. He is said to have interviewed about a thousand shaykhs and examined more than 200,000 hadiths. His principal collection, *Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī*, was compiled in 846 and selected 7,563 narrations, including repetitions, from over 600,000; fewer than 3,000 remain once repeats are excluded. It is arranged by subject in 97 "books" subdivided into 3,450 chapters. With the collection of his student [[Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj]], it forms the Ṣaḥīḥayn, regarded by Sunnis as the principal compilations of reliable hadith. Late in life he was exiled from Nishapur and settled at Khartank, near [[Samarkand]].

Arab Muslim scholar and reformer from [[Najd]] in the [[Arabian Peninsula]], considered the eponymous founder of the Wahhabi movement. Trained in the Hanbali school, he insisted that Muslims return directly to the [[Quran]] and [[Hadith]] rather than rely on medieval legal manuals, and he called for ijtihad (independent legal reasoning). He condemned the veneration of tombs and shrines of Muslim [[Saint|saints]] as heretical innovation. His call for reform rested on the doctrine of tawhid (oneness of God) and drew on the treatises of [[Ibn Taymiyya]]. He allied with Muhammad bin Saud to establish the Emirate of Diriyah, the first Saudi state. The alliance between their families continues in [[Saudi Arabia]], where his descendants, the Al ash-Sheikh, have historically led the clerical establishment.

Ghurid ruler who extended Islamic rule into northern India. Based in the Ghur region of present-day central [[Afghanistan]], Muhammad ruled from 1173 and shared power with his elder brother Ghiyath al-Din until the latter's death in 1203. Crossing the [[Indus River]] in 1175, he captured [[Multan]] within a year, and by 1186 he had uprooted the Ghaznavids and conquered most of [[Punjab]]. After a defeat at Tarain in 1191, he returned a year later and won a decisive victory on the same battlefield, then executed [[Prithviraj Chauhan]]. He left Indian campaigns largely to elite slave commanders, whose conquests laid the foundations of the [[Delhi Sultanate]]. He was assassinated by Isma'ili emissaries on the Indus while offering evening prayers.

Indian businessman, chairman and managing director of Reliance Industries. Born in [[Aden]], he is the son of [[Dhirubhai Ambani]], who founded Reliance. He left a [[Stanford University|Stanford]] MBA in 1980 to help build the company, and he oversaw the construction of its largest petroleum refinery at Jamnagar. After his father's death in 2002, the group's companies were divided between him and his younger brother, Anil Ambani. He later expanded the group into finance, healthcare, media, telecommunications and sports. Critics have pointed to reports of market manipulation and cronyism.

Domestic equine hybrid, offspring of a male [[Donkey|donkey]] and a female [[Horse|horse]]. Mules are more patient, hardier and longer-lived than horses, and are perceived as less obstinate and more intelligent than donkeys. Horses have 64 chromosomes and donkeys 62, so a mule's 63 cannot pair properly, and mules are typically sterile. Mules were probably bred in Anatolia and Mesopotamia before 1000 BC, and the [[Hittites]] valued them more highly than their best horses. In the 19th century mules became favored draft animals on farms, and from 1883 to 1889 teams of 18 mules and two horses hauled borax out of [[Death Valley]], California. Their use declined in industrialized countries in the second half of the 20th century, as [[Tractor|tractors]] replaced them.

Surrealist neo-noir mystery film written and directed by [[David Lynch]], released in 2001. It follows an aspiring actress who befriends an amnesiac woman in [[Los Angeles]], intertwined with a Hollywood director's clash with criminal interference. The film began as a television pilot for ABC, shot in 1999, but the network canceled it after viewing Lynch's cut. Lynch then secured funding from StudioCanal and wrote a new ending. Its events are left open to interpretation. It earned Lynch the Best Director award at the [[Cannes Film Festival]] and an Academy Award nomination for Best Director. It grossed $20.1 million on a $15 million budget.

Iranian Twelver Shia philosopher, theologian and mystic, active in the 17th century under the [[Safavid dynasty]]. Born in [[Shiraz]] to a family of court officials, he is regarded as the master of the Illuminationist school of philosophy. He synthesized [[Avicenna|Avicennism]], the Illuminationism of Suhrawardi, the Sufi metaphysics of [[Ibn Arabi]] and Sunni Ash'ari theology into a Twelver framework, which he called Transcendent Theosophy and set out in *The Transcendent Philosophy of the Four Journeys of the Intellect*. He emphasized the primacy of existence over essence, and scholars credit him with a major shift from essentialism to existentialism in Islamic philosophy. According to Oliver Leaman, he is arguably the most important philosopher in the Muslim world in the last 400 years.

Family of about 78 species of coastal ray-finned fish (*Mugilidae*), found in temperate and tropical waters worldwide, with some species in fresh water. Mullets have two separate dorsal fins, small triangular mouths and no lateral line organ, and most feed on detritus with unusually muscular stomachs. Mullets have been an important food in Mediterranean Europe since [[Ancient Rome|Roman]] times, and in [[Ancient Egypt]] they were eaten pickled and dried as fesikh. Indigenous communities in [[Florida]], [[Hawaii]] and [[North Carolina]] fished them from as far back as the 15th century. Many species leap from the water, and the reasons for the slower, turning leap are disputed, though it may help them gain oxygen-rich air. In the 1960s Florida officials tried to revive demand with a campaign to rename mullet "lisa".

City in the [[Punjab]] province of [[Pakistan]], on the eastern bank of the Chenab River, and one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in Asia. It was besieged by [[Alexander the Great]] during the Mallian campaign in 326 BC. The Umayyad commander Muhammad bin Qasim conquered it in 712, and in the 9th century it became capital of the Emirate of Multan. It was capital of the Langah Sultanate from 1445. After reforms of [[Akbar]] in 1580, Multan became one of the largest provinces of the [[Mughal Empire]]. The [[Sikh Empire]] ruled it from 1818 until the British captured it in 1849 after a lengthy siege. Attracting many Sufi mystics in the 11th and 12th centuries, the city is known as the "City of Saints" for its many shrines.

Method of computer access control, also called two-factor authentication (2FA), in which a user must present two or more distinct types of evidence, or factors, to gain access. Factors include something the user has, such as a phone or security token; something the user knows, such as a [[Password]]; and something the user is, such as a [[Fingerprint]]. Accounts with MFA enabled are significantly less likely to be compromised. Attacks that can bypass it include fatigue attacks, [[Phishing]] and SIM swapping. Physical security keys are generally the most secure option, while [[SMS]] is the most commonly used.

Coexistence of multiple cultures in one society, a term used in [[Sociology|sociology]], political philosophy and everyday speech. In political science it describes a state's capacity to deal with cultural plurality within its borders, and it has been described as a "salad bowl" rather than a melting pot. Canada adopted multiculturalism as national policy in 1971, and [[Australia]] followed in 1973. Supporters argue that it reduces overt discrimination and enriches society. Critics cite research such as Harvard political scientist Robert Putnam's 2007 analysis of over 30,000 U.S. respondents, which found that greater ethnic diversity correlated with lower interpersonal trust. In 2010 German chancellor [[Angela Merkel]] declared that the approach had "utterly failed", and Denmark and the [[Netherlands]] have since moved toward civic integration requirements. The [[Achaemenid Empire]] under [[Cyrus the Great]] also tolerated many cultures.

Use of more than one language by an individual or a group of speakers. Two languages are called bilingualism, and people who speak several are called polyglots. More than half of all Europeans claim to speak at least one language other than their mother tongue, and multilingual speakers are believed to outnumber monolinguals worldwide. Vivian Cook has argued that most multilingual speakers fall between minimal and maximal definitions, and calls them "multi-competent." What counts as a distinct language can change for political reasons: Serbo-Croatian was standardized and, after the [[Breakup of Yugoslavia]], split into Serbian, Croatian, Bosnian and Montenegrin. In [[Finland]], children must learn at least three languages. [[Singapore]] promotes four languages, English, Mandarin, Malay and Tamil, for national cohesion.

Form of communication that combines text, audio, images, animation and [[Video|video]] in a single presentation, unlike traditional mass media such as printed material or audio recordings, which carry one form of content. Examples include video podcasts, audio slideshows and animated videos. Content can also be generated by algorithmic or artificial intelligence systems in response to user input. The term was coined in 1966 by singer and artist Bob Goldstein to promote his show *Lightworks at L'Oursin* in Southampton, New York. By the 1990s it had taken on its current meaning, and hypermedia extensions brought multimedia to the World Wide Web. Multimedia can be played on computers, [[Smartphone|smartphones]] and other devices.

Definite [[Integral|integral]] of a function of several real variables, such as f(x, y) or f(x, y, z). Integrals of a function of two variables over a region in the plane are called double integrals, and those of three variables over a region in space are triple integrals. The double integral of a positive function gives the volume between its surface and the plane of its domain, just as a single definite integral gives an [[Area|area]]. Multiple integrals are defined as limits of Riemann sums over partitions of the domain. They are computed as iterated single integrals by [[Fubini's theorem]], integrating one variable at a time. They are used in [[Physics]] and engineering, for example to calculate centers of mass and moments of inertia, and in probability to compute expectations for multivariate distributions.

Cancer of plasma cells, a type of [[White blood cell|white blood cell]] that normally produces [[Antibody|antibodies]]. It often causes no symptoms at first; as it progresses, it can cause bone pain, [[Anemia]], kidney problems and infections. Risk factors include [[Obesity]] and radiation exposure, and the disease almost always develops from a precancerous stage called monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance. Diagnosis relies on blood or urine tests, a [[Biopsy|bone marrow biopsy]] and imaging. It is treatable but generally incurable; [[Steroid|steroids]], [[Chemotherapy]] and stem cell transplant can bring remission. About 175,000 people were diagnosed globally in 2020.

Chronic, neurodegenerative autoimmune disease of the [[Central nervous system|central nervous system]], in which the immune system attacks myelin, the insulating covering of nerve cells, impairing the transmission of signals. Symptoms depend on lesion location and may include double vision, vision loss, numbness, muscle weakness, [[Ataxia|loss of coordination]] and memory problems. Fatigue is among the most common symptoms. Diagnosis relies on symptoms, [[Magnetic resonance imaging|MRI]] scans and sometimes a [[Lumbar puncture|lumbar puncture]]. There is no cure, but disease-modifying therapies can reduce attacks, and [[Physical therapy]] helps manage symptoms. Life expectancy is slightly lower than normal. The disease usually begins between ages 20 and 40 and is almost three times more common in women than in men. It was first described in 1868 by French neurologist Jean-Martin Charcot.

Arithmetic operation that combines two factors to produce a product. It is one of the four elementary operations of arithmetic, along with addition, subtraction and [[Division (mathematics)|division]], and is the inverse of division. For whole numbers it can be understood as repeated addition, so 3 × 4 equals 4 + 4 + 4 or 3 + 3 + 3 + 3. Multiplication is [[Commutative property|commutative]]: the order of the factors does not change the product. It extends to [[Integer]]s, [[Rational number]]s and [[Real number]]s, and the product of two measurements carries a derived unit, so multiplying the sides of a rectangle gives its area in square meters. [[Ancient Egypt|Ancient Egyptians]] used a doubling method, and [[Brahmagupta]] formalized its rules in the Hindu–Arabic system. Some extensions, such as [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] multiplication, are not commutative.

Extension of [[Calculus|calculus]] to functions of several variables, covering their differentiation and integration rather than one variable alone. A special case in three-dimensional space is often called [[Vector calculus]]. Partial [[Derivative|derivatives]] measure how a function changes with respect to one variable while the others are held constant. Generalizing to several variables introduces difficulties: a limit can depend on the path along which a point is approached, and continuity in each variable separately does not guarantee continuity overall. Several types of integration exist, including line, surface and volume integrals, so an antiderivative cannot be defined uniquely. Theorems such as Green's theorem, Stokes' theorem and the divergence theorem relate these integrals to [[Flux|flux]] and circulation. The subject is used in physics, [[Engineering]] and [[Economics]].

Probability distribution that generalizes the one-dimensional [[Normal distribution|normal distribution]] to higher dimensions. A random vector is multivariate normal if every linear combination of its components has a univariate normal distribution. Also called the multivariate Gaussian or joint normal distribution, it is described by a mean vector and a covariance matrix. Its importance derives mainly from the [[Central limit theorem|multivariate central limit theorem]]. It is often used to describe, at least approximately, any set of correlated real-valued [[Random variable|random variables]] that cluster around a mean value.

Hypothetical set of all [[Universe|universes]], presumed to comprise everything that exists, including all space, time, matter, energy and physical laws. Its universes are variously called parallel universes or many worlds. Some physicists regard it as a philosophical notion rather than a scientific hypothesis, because it cannot be empirically falsified, and searches for evidence have found no statistically significant support. Max Tegmark's four-level classification includes universes with different physical constants and the [[Many-worlds interpretation|many-worlds interpretation]] of quantum mechanics. The [[Anthropic principle]] suggests that many universes with different physical laws could explain the apparent fine-tuning of this universe for conscious life.

[[Rapid transit|Rapid transit]] system serving [[Mumbai]] and its metropolitan region in [[Maharashtra]], India. As of April 2026 it had 4 color-coded lines with 77 stations and 91.48 km of track, and 16 lines are planned. Construction began in February 2008, and the Blue Line, the first, opened on June 8, 2014. Its lines are underground, at-grade and elevated. It is India's third-largest and third-busiest metro system.
